title: Counting Sort
oneLiner: When the values fall in a small range, count how many times each value appears and write them back in order. O(n + k), no comparisons at all.
keyTakeaway: Comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n), but counting sort does not compare: it tallies each value in an array indexed by value (offset by the minimum) and then reads the tallies in order. O(n + k) time and O(k) space, where k is the range max - min + 1, so it wins when k is not much bigger than n.
explanation:
Return nums sorted in ascending order using counting sort. The values may be negative, but the range from the smallest to the largest is small.

Every sort so far compares elements, and it can be proved that any comparison sort needs about n log n comparisons in the worst case. Counting sort sidesteps that by using the values themselves as array indices. Find min and max, make counts of size k = max - min + 1, and for each x add one to counts[x - min] (the offset maps min to index 0, which also handles negatives). Then walk counts from left to right and write value i + min out counts[i] times.

Both passes are linear: O(n) to count and O(n + k) to write out, so O(n + k) total, with O(k) for the counts. That is excellent for exam scores 0 to 100, ages, or bytes 0 to 255. It is terrible when the range is huge: sorting [1, 1000000000] would allocate a billion counters. That trade between n and k is the whole decision.

Counting sort is also the building block of radix sort, which sorts large integers by running a stable counting sort on one digit at a time. For that, the write-out phase uses prefix sums of the counts to find each value's position, which keeps equal keys in their original order. Bucket sort is the related idea for real numbers spread evenly over a range.

The visualization sorts [4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1]: the array shows the counts as they build up, then the output.

recognitionSignals: Integers in a small known range (scores, ages, letters a to z, digits).
"Sort in linear time" or "faster than n log n": only possible without comparisons.
Frequency counting of bounded values, then producing them in order (the same counts array feeds Top K Frequent with bucket sort).
gotchas: Forgetting the min offset: negative values give a negative index.
k is max - min + 1, not max - min; the top value needs a slot too.
Handle the empty array before calling min and max.
confusableWith: Comparison sorts (merge, quick, heap) work for any values in O(n log n); counting sort only works for small integer ranges but runs in O(n + k).
A hash map of counts (Word Frequency) also tallies values, but has no order; counting sort's array is indexed by value, so reading it left to right is sorted order.

complexity.note: Here k is the range max - min + 1. One O(n) pass fills the counts and one O(n + k) pass writes the output. The counts array is O(k) (the output is another O(n)). When k is about n this is linear; when k is huge it is worse than any comparison sort.
